svg.title: Five defensive tiers on one request path, and the condition that makes layering work
svg.desc: A request descends through five tiers in order: edge, network, identity, application, and data. Each tier row names its controls and states what an attacker still holds after that tier is bypassed. An arrow runs down the left side marking the attacker's path. A footer states that layering only reduces the likelihood of systemic compromise when the tiers fail for largely independent reasons, and that stacking controls which share a parsing or detection weakness gives correlated failure rather than depth.
svg.text: Five tiers on one request path
A tier is only a layer if it fails for a different reason than the tier above it.
WAF payload filtering, cloud DDoS mitigation, TLS termination. Bypassed by novel encodings: the request still reaches the network.
Microsegmentation, default-deny security groups, egress proxy. Bypassed from an allowed peer: reachability is not authorization.
Phishing-resistant MFA, scoped tokens, short sessions. Bypassed by a stolen live session: the caller now looks legitimate.
Parameterized queries, per-object authorization, output encoding. Bypassed by a logic flaw: the app acts with its own credentials.
Envelope encryption, row-level security, append-only audit logs. Encryption at rest does not stop an app entitled to decrypt.
Layering lowers the likelihood that one failure becomes systemic compromise. It does not eliminate it, and it only helps when the tiers
fail for largely independent reasons. Two engines sharing one parser fail together, which is duplication rather than depth.
Count independent failure modes, not boxes on the diagram.
